title: Θύννος καὶ δελφίς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 132. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Θύννος διωκόμενος ὑπὸ δελφῖνος καὶ πολλῷ τῷ ῥοίζῳ φερόμενος, ἐπειδὴ καταλαμβάνεσθαι ἔμελλεν, ἔλαθεν ὑπὸ σφοδρᾶς ὁρμῆς ἐκβρασθεὶς εἴς τινα ἠϊόνα.
sentences.tr: Thynnos diōkomenos hypo delphinos kai pollōi tōi rhoizōi pheromenos, epeidē katalambanesthai emellen, elathen hypo sphodras hormēs ekbrastheis eis tina ēiona.
sentences.l: A tuna, being pursued by a dolphin and being borne along with a great rushing, when he was about to be overtaken, escaped his own notice being flung up by a violent onrush onto a certain beach.
sentences.i: A tuna was being chased by a dolphin and driven on with a great rushing of the water; and just as he was about to be overtaken, the force of the rush flung him, before he knew it, onto a beach.
sentences.n: ἔλαθεν … ἐκβρασθείς is λανθάνω with a supplementary participle: the participle carries what happened, the finite verb says it happened unnoticed. English has to turn the pair inside out — 'he was flung up without noticing it'. The same construction returns twice in the fowler's fable. ῥοῖζος is the whistling rush of something moving fast through air or water. ὑπὸ σφοδρᾶς ὁρμῆς names no owner: whether the onrush is the tuna's own flight or the dolphin's charge is left open.

sentences.t: Ὑπὸ δὲ τῆς αὐτῆς φορᾶς ἐλαυνόμενος καὶ ὁ δελφὶς αὐτῷ συνεξώσθη.
sentences.tr: Hypo de tēs autēs phoras elaunomenos kai ho delphis autōi synexōsthē.
sentences.l: And the dolphin too, driven by the same rush, was shoved out along with him.
sentences.n: καί stands before ὁ δελφίς and means 'the dolphin as well'. συνεξωθέω is ἐξωθέω, 'shove out', with συν- for the company: one shove carries the two of them out of the water onto the same beach.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ θύννος, ὡς ἐθεάσατο ἐπιστραφεὶς αὐτὸν λιποθυμοῦντα ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἔμοιγε οὐκέτι λυπηρὸς ὁ θάνατος· ὁρῶ γὰρ καὶ τὸν αἴτιόν μοι θανάτου γενόμενον συναποθνῄσκοντα. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho thynnos, hōs etheasato epistrapheis auton lipothymounta ephē· « All’ emoige ouketi lypēros ho thanatos· horō gar kai ton aition moi thanatou genomenon synapothnēiskonta. »
sentences.l: And the tuna, when, having turned about, he beheld him fainting away, said: « Well, to me at any rate death is no longer painful; for I see even the one who became the cause of death for me dying along with me. »
sentences.i: And the tuna turned about, and when he saw him swooning, said: « Well then, death is no grief to me now; for I see the very one who became the cause of my death dying along with me. »
sentences.n: ὁρῶ takes a supplementary participle, συναποθνῄσκοντα, for what is seen happening — the regular construction after verbs of perceiving. λιποθυμέω is 'to leave one's spirit behind', the word for a swoon. καὶ τὸν αἴτιον is 'the very one who was the cause'. ἔμοιγε is the dative of the person concerned with γε for emphasis: 'to me at any rate, whatever it is to others'.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι ῥᾴδιον φέρουσι τὰς συμφορὰς οἱ ἄνθρωποι, ὅταν ἴδωσι καὶ τοὺς αἰτίους τούτων γεγονότας δυστυχοῦντας.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti rhaidion pherousi tas symphoras hoi anthrōpoi, hotan idōsi kai tous aitious toutōn gegonotas dystychountas.
sentences.l: The story shows that men bear their misfortunes easily, whenever they see the very ones who became the causes of them faring badly as well.
sentences.n: ῥᾴδιον is a neuter adjective standing in for an adverb, 'easily'. ὅταν with the subjunctive ἴδωσι is the indefinite 'whenever', of a thing that holds any time it happens. καί here goes with τοὺς αἰτίους: the causes too, and not only the sufferers. Both γεγονότας and δυστυχοῦντας hang on ἴδωσι as participles of what is seen.
